Let X be the number of balls ahead of the chosen ball.
If X≥3 then after one piston fires
  • with probability 1/3 one ball is removed (X→X−1)
  • with probability 2/3 two balls are removed (X→X−2)
When X∈{0,1,2} the ball is on the platform:
  X=0 (position 1): P=1/3
  X=1 (position 2): P=5/9
  X=2 (position 3): P=17/27
Thus for X≥3 the ejection probability satisfies
    f(X)= (1/3)f(X−1)+(2/3)f(X−2)
Solving this recurrence with the above bases gives
    f(X)= 3/5 + (1/15)(−2/3)^X   for X≥1
For ball n (n≥2) X=n−1, so
    P(n)= 3/5 + (1/15)(−2/3)^{n−1}
This oscillates about 0.6 and decreases in amplitude as n grows.  The maximum occurs at n=3:
    P(3)=17/27≈0.6296 › P(n) for all n≠3
Ball 1 has probability 1/3, lower than ball 3.
Therefore the ball with the greatest chance of being ejected is ball number 3.
Label p1, p2, p3 as the probabilities that a ball now sitting in platform positions 1, 2 or 3 is eventually struck by a piston.

• If a ball is in position 1 it is struck next turn with probability 1⁄3, otherwise it rolls away, so p1 = 1⁄3.
• If a ball is in position 2: with probability 1⁄3 it is struck immediately; with probability 2⁄3 a different piston fires and the ball moves to position 1, after which its chance is p1.  Hence p2 = (1⁄3)·1 + (2⁄3)·p1 = 1⁄3 + (2⁄3)(1⁄3) = 5⁄9.
• If a ball is in position 3: with probability 1⁄3 it is struck immediately; with probability 1⁄3 it moves to position 1 (chance p1); with probability 1⁄3 it moves to position 2 (chance p2).  Therefore
  p3 = (1⁄3)·1 + (1⁄3)·p1 + (1⁄3)·p2 =
        1⁄3 + 1⁄9 + 5⁄27 = 17⁄27.

Every ball numbered 3 or higher first appears on the platform in position 3, so its chance of being piston-ejected is 17⁄27 ≈ 0.6296, greater than the chances for balls 1 (1⁄3) or 2 (5⁄9).

Thus any ball numbered 3 – 100 is optimal; choosing the earliest of these is customary.

Let H be the number of humans and V the number of vampires, with H + V = 100.

Each resident says: “At least one of us is a human.”

Truth value of the statement:
• True if H ≥ 1.
• False if H = 0.

1. Suppose H ≥ 1 (statement true).
   – Humans (truth-tellers) could say it.
   – Vampires (liars) could not say a true statement.
   – But everyone gives the same statement, so there could be no vampires.
   – This would give V = 0, contradicting the sighting of a vampire.

2. Therefore H = 0.
   – The statement is false.
   – All residents are lying, consistent only if they are all vampires.

Thus V = 100.
All one hundred residents give identical statement “At least one of us is a human.” If even one human were present, the sentence would be true, so vampires (who must lie) could not utter it, contradicting the uniform reply. Therefore the statement must be false, meaning there are no humans. Consequently every resident is a vampire, totaling one hundred vampires.

Let Bob’s three guesses be g1,g2,g3 (non-negative integers).  Sort them so g1≤g2≤g3.

Host’s objective is to choose a triple (a,b,c) of coin counts that
  • sums to 30,
  • contains a pair whose counts differ by exactly 6,
  • has at least one box with ≥2 coins,
  • after a permutation gives Bob the least possible payoff  Σ min(gi, ai) where each term is taken only if gi≤ai (otherwise it is 0).

1.  Equal guesses are never worse for Bob than unequal guesses.  Any unequal-guess strategy can be converted to the common value g=⌊(g1+g2+g3)/3⌋ without decreasing the minimum guaranteed payoff, because the host can always permute the boxes so that the largest guess is matched with the smallest coin count, the second largest with the middle count, etc.  Hence we may assume Bob uses the uniform strategy (g,g,g).

2.  For a fixed g the worst case for Bob is when as few boxes as possible contain at least g coins.  If every box holds fewer than g coins Bob earns nothing; if exactly one box contains at least g coins he earns g; if two or three boxes do, he earns 2g or 3g.

3.  Determine for every g how many boxes the host can keep below g.
    •  g≥13: the host can put at most 12 coins in every box (e.g. 12,12,6), maintaining a 6-difference, so Bob could be held to 0.  Therefore g≥13 is useless.
    •  g=12: can the host keep every box below 12?  No.  To keep all boxes ≤11 their total would be ≤33, and with the 6-difference requirement this is impossible (previous exhaustive enumeration shows no such triple).  The host can, however, arrange that exactly one box is ≥12, e.g. (13,7,10).  Thus Bob is guaranteed to have at least one winning box and exactly one in the worst case, giving him 12 coins.
    •  g≤11: since 30=3·10, the host can arrange all three boxes to be below or equal to g, e.g. for g=11 use (11,11,8) with difference 3—not acceptable.  Using the exhaustive list of valid triples we see that for every g≤11 the host can place all three boxes below g (e.g. g=11→(12,12,6) impossible; g=11 actually must pay something).  Checking g=11 specifically: the host can use (12,12,6) but 12>11 so two boxes are ≥g, guaranteeing Bob 22.  Yet Bob could instead have chosen g=12 and guaranteed 12 while exposing himself to no higher minimum with g smaller than 12.  Consequently, g=12 gives the best worst-case payoff.

Hence Bob’s optimal strategy is to guess 12,12,12, guaranteeing he receives at least 12 coins.  Since each coin is worth $1,000, the minimum amount of money Bob can force is 12×1,000.
Let Bob’s three guesses be sorted g1 ≤ g2 ≤ g3 and let the host’s coin counts (after shuffling) be sorted a1 ≤ a2 ≤ a3 with a1 + a2 + a3 = 30, one pair differing by 6.

1.  An upper bound on any guaranteed gain
   •  The host can choose the distribution (0, 6, 24).
   •  Against Bob’s worst-case ordering the host pairs g3→0, g2→6, g1→24.
   •  Bob’s payoff is then 0 + [g2 if g2≤6 else 0] + [g1 if g1≤24 else 0] ≤ 6 + g1.
   •  Because g1 ≤ g2 ≤ 6 in the above case, the maximum possible total is 12.
   → No strategy can guarantee more than 12 coins.

2.  A strategy that guarantees 12 coins
   •  Bob guesses (6, 6, 6).
   •  Any legal distribution must have at least two boxes containing ≥6 coins (if only one box had ≥6, the two smaller boxes would both be <6 and could not differ from each other or from the large box by exactly 6).
   •  Therefore at least two of Bob’s guesses are ≤ the corresponding coin counts, giving him 2 × 6 = 12 coins no matter how the host distributes or permutes the coins.

3.  Optimal guaranteed amount
   •  Step 1 shows 12 coins is the largest guarantee possible.
   •  Step 2 shows Bob can actually secure 12 coins.

Hence the optimal strategy guarantees 12 coins, each worth $1,000, so the minimum amount of money Bob can be sure to win is 12,000.
